en: 1. *Pañcākāra* by Bhaṭṭārakaratnākara = first item in NAK 1-1697 5/0 vi. bauddhatantra 30 = NGMPP B 31/6 (2r1–3r3) 2. *Pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi* (anonymous) = second item in NAK 1-1697 5/0 vi. bauddhatantra 30 = NGMPP B 31/6 (3r3–8r1) 3. *Caturmudrānvaya* by Advayavajra = third item in NAK 1-1697 5/0 vi. bauddhatantra 30 = NGMPP B 31/6 (8r1–*14)
4. *Guhyāvalī* of Dauḍīpāda = fourth item in NAK 1-1697 5/0 vi. bauddhatantra 30 = NGMPP B 31/6 (*14 -29(!?)r1) 5. An unidentified work in the *Pañcakrama* tradition:
*Namaḥ śrīvajrasattvāya* (Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva).
Having realized the true nature of the winds through the power of the reality of mantra, being free from the formalities of speech due to the yoga of mental contemplation,
he beholds the path of the three realms as being empty in its very essence.
May this vajra-recitation bestow happiness upon you. || 1 ||
When the multitude of beings was terrified, perceiving that the vital breaths were being obstructed within the life-force wind by the ninefold wind,
the Lord of Life, whose nature is self-experience, [became] the knower of the paths.
Having released the long sound, it attains a state equal to space. || 2 ||

Victorious is the lion of great bliss, white as the luster of the autumn moon, who, having cast off the herd of elephants— the objects of the senses— upon the peak of the mountain whose summits are the *vasu* [eight], reigns supreme.
Then the wise Lord, whose abode is the wind, traveled from his head to the pair of his feet and reached his heart,
like a lion roaming through a forest of non-origination that is the limit of all beings.
Blessed are those practitioners of mantra who, through their very distinct [practice], attain the radiant abode white as the nectar of the moon; for they have indeed acquired merit. || 5 ||
When the Lord, the master of the vital breaths, has dissolved into the self alone; when the multitude of inhalations and exhalations has come to rest and the life-wind is restrained—
then that [reality] which is more luminous than even birth belongs to the masters of yoga.
Devouring his own limbs, he, whose body is beneficial, traverses the three worlds.
With the eyes fixed on the tip of the nose, the vital breaths properly controlled, and the tongue placed against the palate while the lips are joined,
[the yogis] become wise ones as bright as the moon, their masses of darkness destroyed by the light of knowledge.
Those free from conceptual thought perceive this world as entirely empty and without abode.
With their teeth touching teeth like restrained tender sprouts, they behold the world as luminous with their eyes cast downward. (8)

For embodied beings whose minds are free from the distinction between passion and dispassion, these are the destroyers of afflictions; equal to those whose minds are purified by the destruction of illusion and delusion, they consist of the cessation that dispels the void of thought; they are the protectors arisen through mantra.
The wise perceive the mind as heaven, the mortal world, and even the abode of the serpent-king.
The darkness cast away by the flames of the fire of play that transcends thought;
the imperishable ones who dwell in the beautiful abode of the power liberated from merit and demerit; the foremost of the practitioners of the *samaya*, the yogins—[they are] clear and pure.
They perceive the supramundane, which is without abode, within the body of the Victor. || 10 ||

In this essence-less [world], the fortunate ones attain within their own bodies that which is the supreme essence, eternal within what is subject to momentary destruction—the one whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest. (11)
Having conquered the Great Hero, he who was skilled in the application of the ministers' counsel enjoyed the entire collection of territories and rendered the world empty. 12.
He for whom the distinction between the even and the uneven is no longer perceived,
and in whom indeed the notions of eternalism and nihilism have not arisen;
he has cast off all conceptual constructions and is liberated from the birth of imagination.
He is victorious, the one united in yuganaddha, whose intrinsic nature is the state of Buddhahood. || 13 ||
Indeed, his [bow] was firm, possessed of many branches, with a shimmering web of rays,
equal in brilliance to the moon and sun, radiant, fearless,
and truly endowed with excellent qualities. 15.
Even poison is equal to nectar, and its fruit is exceedingly charming; who would not resort to that which is as essence-less as the core of a plantain tree? 16.
Those with divine vision behold the entire universe as being like the moon reflected in water, a mirage, a cloud, a city of the Gandharvas, and a magical illusion. 17.
Earth, water, fire, air, and ether— by these five elements,

which are honored by Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, this world was produced; it is praised for its forms and other qualities, and through the excellent restraint of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), it has become radiant with light.
O Goddess who sports in the five wisdoms, [you are] the awakened ones... || 18 ||
All this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, is like an illusion and a dream— thus one should contemplate.
